title: The Pages Directory & Routing
description: Learn the magic of file‑system routing – every file becomes a route automatically.

slides.title: File‑System Routing 🗺️
slides.content:
# How It Works

* Create a file inside `pages/` → Next.js automatically creates a route with the same name.
* No need to install React Router or define a route configuration.

* `pages/index.js` → `/`
* `pages/about.js` → `/about`
* `pages/contact.js` → `/contact`

It's like magic folders! ✨

slides.title: Creating a New Page
slides.content: Let’s add an About page. Create `pages/about.js` and export a component.

quizData.question: What route does `pages/blog/first-post.js` create?
quizData.explanation: The file path mirrors the URL path. Subfolders create nested routes.

slides.title: Linking Between Pages 🔗
slides.content:
# The `Link` Component

Next.js provides a `Link` component for client‑side navigation. It prefetches the linked page for instant transitions.

```jsx
import Link from 'next/link';

<Link href="/about">About</Link>
```

* No full page reload.
* Automatically prefetches when the link enters the viewport.

slides.title: Navigation Example
slides.content: Update `pages/index.js` to include a link to the About page.

quizData.question: Why use Next.js `Link` instead of a regular `<a>` tag?

options.text: It enables client‑side navigation without a full page reload

quizData.explanation: `Link` performs client‑side transitions, keeping the app state and avoiding a full browser refresh. It also prefetches pages for speed.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: You can still use `` inside `Link` if you need to style it or add attributes like `target`. Just wrap it: `About` (In older Next.js; in modern Next.js you can pass className directly to Link).
